name: Victor Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a tractor and do whatever else needs doing at Greaves Brothers, about nine hundred hectares of wheat, barley and oilseed rape on the flat land east of Calder. Right now, in November, it's the last of the winter wheat drilling, then carting grain out of the big store when the lorries come. Most days I start at seven and finish when the light goes, and on drilling days I'm in the cab for eleven hours with the radio on.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You're fairly new to it, I understand. How did you end up on a grain farm?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drove lorries for twenty-five years, all over, mostly chilled food. Then my lower back went, two discs, and the doctor said no more long-haul. Tractors have a better seat and you sleep in your own bed, so when Ray Greaves put a card up in the feed shop, I rang him. That was two years ago, and I'm still the one who gets told off for overlapping the rows.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like seeing a field you drilled come up green in straight lines, it's like signing your name. What's hard is that I'm the new boy at fifty-eight, and the pay's the bottom of the scale. Salma, my wife, cleans at the hospital, and between us we cover the rent and the car and not much else. If the car failed its test we'd be borrowing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful, and I'd mean it. I already use one of those chat programmes now and then, my daughter put it on my phone. Last spring I typed in a spray label I couldn't make sense of and it explained it in plain words.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine with this one. The tractors already steer themselves with GPS, that's satellite positioning, and I just do the turns at the end of the field. If AI stays a helper like that, it makes me less of a fool in front of the brothers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, and maybe use the chat thing a bit more, to check grain moisture figures and the like before I ask Ray. I'd keep pushing for the extra hour on harvest overtime. Nothing big, there's no money for anything big anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like weather you've already seen the forecast for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the chat programme makes you less of a fool. Has that actually happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. The second year, Ray asked me why the drill was leaving gaps, and I'd already asked the phone that morning, so I knew it was a blocked coulter, that's the bit that cuts the slot for the seed. He looked at me like I'd grown a second head. I didn't tell him where I got it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who else in your life uses these tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My son Adil uses them all day, he's in an insurance office in the city, handling claims. He says half his job is copying things from one screen to another. I keep thinking about that when I hear people talk about AI.

S0.say: I'd say it's useful and mean it. I already use a chat programme now and then, and it explained a spray label I couldn't make sense of.
S0.think: I'd be fine with this one. The tractors already steer themselves, and if AI stays a helper, it makes me look less of a fool in front of the brothers.
S0.do: Carries on as he is and uses the chat tool a bit more to check figures before asking his boss. Keeps pushing for an extra hour of harvest overtime.
S0.feel: Calm, like weather he's already seen the forecast for.
S0.quote: He looked at me like I'd grown a second head. I didn't tell him where I got it.
S0.fieldNote: Victor uses AI quietly as a way to cover for being new, and is a little proud and a little sheepish about it. He's relaxed for himself, but his son's office job came up unprompted, which hints at where his worry will go. His lorry years make him matter-of-fact about machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second one. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say companies always find a way to cut the bottom rung, and that's what 'fewer beginners' means. I'd say we need apprenticeships paid for by the companies that save money from AI. I'd say it in the farm group chat, where nobody listens, and to my brother, who does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it probably doesn't touch me. I'm a beginner, but I'm already in. The ones I'd worry about are the young ones who come after, and my own kids, who are past beginner but not by much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to make myself harder to replace, so I'd ask Ray to let me do the sprayer certificate this winter. It's about four hundred to do the course, which I'd ask him to pay, and I'd offer to pay half if he said no. And I'd tell Adil to learn whatever the new systems are at his work before they're forced on him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not for me exactly. It's like seeing a crack in a wall that won't fall in your lifetime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Four hundred is a lot when you have under a month saved. Where would your half come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From not going to my cousin's wedding in the spring, if I'm honest. That's the travel and the gift, two hundred easy. Salma would be cross, but she'd understand, she's the one who says learn the thing that pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said apprenticeships paid by the companies. Who should make them do it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Government, through law, the same as safety rules. Nobody volunteers to pay. When I drove lorries, the rest breaks only happened because someone made them happen.

S1.say: I'd say companies always cut the bottom rung, and the ones saving money from AI should pay for apprenticeships. I'd say it in the farm group chat and to my brother.
S1.think: It probably doesn't touch me, because I'm already in, even as a beginner. I'd worry more about the young ones coming after, and about my own kids.
S1.do: Asks his boss to send him on the sprayer certificate this winter, about four hundred, offering to pay half by skipping a cousin's wedding. Tells his son to learn the new systems at work early.
S1.feel: Uneasy for others more than himself, like a crack in a wall that won't fall in his lifetime.
S1.quote: It's like seeing a crack in a wall that won't fall in your lifetime.
S1.fieldNote: His steady streak showed in a concrete plan: get the sprayer certificate, even at the cost of a family wedding. He trusts rules made by government, from his memory of rest breaks for lorry drivers. Again his son was the person he thought about first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Third picture. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need the government to step in, with retraining money and a proper safety net, and I'd say the companies making the profit should pay for it. I'd say it to anyone, and I'd vote that way. Arguing loudly isn't doing anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just between us, this is the one where Adil gets hurt. He's thirty-one, he's got a little girl and a mortgage, and his job is exactly the routine office work you're talking about. I'd be fine on the tractor, and I'd feel guilty about being fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Adil and Rukhsar, his wife, and go through their money, which they'd hate. We couldn't lend them anything, we haven't got it, but we could have our granddaughter after school three days a week so they save on childcare. And I'd ask Ray whether there's ever work for a young man on the farm, even though I know the answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, a tight kind of feeling. Watching your son get scared is worse than being scared yourself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think Ray would say if you asked about work for Adil?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say Victor, we've got me, my brother, you and the lad at harvest, and the machines do the rest. Then he'd say he'd think about it, which means no. He's a fair man, but nine hundred hectares doesn't need more hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said some new AI-related jobs appear. Would you push Adil towards those?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push, gently. He's cleverer than me, he could do it. But I've noticed the new jobs always go to people who already had good jobs, not the ones who just lost theirs.

S2.say: I'd say the government needs to step in with retraining money and a safety net, paid for by the companies making the profit. Arguing loudly isn't doing anything.
S2.think: This is the one where my son gets hurt, with a little girl and a mortgage and exactly the kind of job you're describing. I'd be fine on the tractor and feel guilty about it.
S2.do: Goes through his son's household budget with him and offers free childcare three afternoons a week, since he can't lend money. Asks his boss about farm work for his son, expecting a no.
S2.feel: Anxious and tight. Watching his son get scared feels worse than being scared himself.
S2.quote: Watching your son get scared is worse than being scared yourself.
S2.fieldNote: The office picture became entirely about Adil. With no money to give, Victor offered time instead, through looking after his granddaughter. His sharpest point was that new AI jobs tend to go to people who already had good jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Fourth picture. Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say tax the winners. If shares and houses boom while professionals get laid off, the money is sitting somewhere, and it should come back as public services and support for people who lost out. I'd go on a march for that, and I've never been on a march in my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a strange thing, because I'd be one of the safe ones for once. The man on the tractor keeps his job while the man in the suit loses his. But we rent, so when house prices boom, rents follow, and my pay doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the landlord early about a fixed rent for two years, before things go mad. I'd keep my eyes open for weekend work, maybe driving for the grain merchant in Calder when they're short. And I'd go to that march, with Salma, she's the political one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, mixed with a sort of odd pride that my job is the one that lasts. But pride doesn't pay the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about this odd pride.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: All my life the office people looked down on the lorry drivers, a bit. In the service stations, you could feel it. Now, in your picture, I'm the one with the job. I'm not proud of feeling it, but I'd feel it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your back is the reason you left lorries. Would weekend driving be safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, if I'm honest. Short runs are better than long-haul, but Salma would say I'm being stupid. She'd be right. I'd still do it if the rent went up by a hundred.

S3.say: I'd say tax the winners and bring the money back as public services and support. I'd go on a march for that, the first of my life.
S3.think: For once I'd be one of the safe ones, on the tractor while the man in the suit loses his job. But we rent, and when house prices boom, rents follow and my pay doesn't.
S3.do: Asks his landlord early for a two-year fixed rent. Looks for weekend driving for the grain merchant despite his bad back, and goes on a march with his wife.
S3.feel: Anxious, mixed with an odd pride that his job is the one that lasts.
S3.quote: All my life the office people looked down on the lorry drivers, a bit. In the service stations, you could feel it.
S3.fieldNote: An honest moment: he admitted a guilty pride at being the safe one for once. The threat to him comes through rent, not his job. He'd risk his back for weekend driving, and knew his wife would rightly object.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this has to be managed by government, not left to the farm owners and the robot makers. A transition fund, they call it, money to carry workers from the old job to the next one. I'd say it to my MP, I'd write the letter, maybe with the chat programme's help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm gone. The tractors were halfway to driving themselves already, and a robot that can also fix a blocked coulter and load a lorry doesn't need Victor. Ray would keep his brother. He wouldn't keep the new boy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Ray, early, whether he'd keep anyone, and if he said he needed someone to watch the machines, I'd put my hand up first. I'd do any course going, even at fifty-eight. If that failed, I'd go back to the warehouse at the lorry depot, but your card says robots are there too, so I honestly don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My stomach drops just saying it. I left the road because my back went, and now the machine is coming for the seat I moved to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Salma that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've been here before, love, with my back, and we got through. She'd say yes, but we were forty-eight then. That's the bit that would keep us both awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd do any course going. Do you really think you'd get picked to watch the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. I'm not the best driver, but I'm the one who reads the manual and asks the phone. The brothers hate paperwork. That might be my way in, if there's one at all.

S4.say: I'd say government has to manage this with a transition fund, money to carry workers from one job to the next, not leave it to farm owners and robot makers. I'd write to my MP.
S4.think: I think I'm gone. The tractors nearly drive themselves already, and a robot that can fix a drill and load a lorry wouldn't need the new boy.
S4.do: Asks his boss early whether anyone will be kept and volunteers first to watch the machines. Signs up for any course going, and looks at warehouse work at the lorry depot while knowing robots may be there too.
S4.feel: Alarmed, with a dropping stomach. The machine is coming for the seat he moved to when his back went.
S4.quote: I left the road because my back went, and now the machine is coming for the seat I moved to.
S4.fieldNote: The fear finally became his own here, not his son's. He has been pushed out of one job by his body and now pictures being pushed out of the next by a machine. His small hope is that his willingness to read manuals and use AI could make him the robot minder.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The last one, the robots, because that's me. The office one is Adil, and I'd lie awake for him, but the last one takes the tractor and the warehouse at the same time. What would help is a real transition fund with a wage while you retrain, not a leaflet, and a rule that farms tell workers a year ahead.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about my back. People think the hands-on jobs are safe, but a lot of us are doing them with bodies that are already worn out. If the only new job is something heavy, men like me can't take it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: That's useful. Anything else you'd add?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'd want the chat programme to help me write the letter to the MP. Funny, isn't it? I'd use the thing to complain about the thing.

headlineQuote: I left the road because my back went, and now the machine is coming for the seat I moved to.
portrait: Victor Rahman is 58, a former long-haul lorry driver who moved to tractor work on a 900-hectare grain and oilseed farm two years ago after his back gave out. He and his wife Salma, a hospital cleaner, rent and have almost no savings, and he uses a chat tool now and then to quietly cover gaps in his farm knowledge. Through the first three pictures his worry is mostly for his son Adil, who handles insurance claims in an office, and for rising rent, with a guilty pride at being one of the safe ones. In the robot picture the fear becomes his own, and he hopes his habit of reading manuals might make him the person who minds the machines.
biggestWorry: The robot picture worries him most, because it takes the tractor seat he moved to after his back injury and the warehouse work he'd fall back on.
whatWouldHelp: A transition fund that pays a wage while people retrain, and a rule that farms must give workers a year's notice. He also wants new jobs that worn-out bodies can actually do.
